related_questions.question: Can GPA be cured?
related_questions.snippet: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a lifelong condition that requires lifelong care. With treatment, the disease can go into remission and stop causing symptoms. But symptoms can also return (relapse). You may have to take medications off and on for the rest of your life to manage relapses.

text_blocks.snippet: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly known as Wegener's granulomatosis, is a rare autoimmune disease that causes inflammation of blood vessels, known as vasculitis. This inflammation can restrict blood flow to tissues and organs, potentially causing damage. GPA is characterized by the formation of granulomas, which are clumps of immune cells, and can affect various parts of the body, particularly the respiratory tract and kidneys.
snippet_highlighted_words: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA), formerly known as Wegener's granulomatosis, is a rare autoimmune disease that causes inflammation of blood vessels, known as vasculitis

list.title: Autoimmune Disease:
list.snippet: GPA is an autoimmune disorder where the body's immune system mistakenly attacks its own healthy tissues, specifically the blood vessels.

list.title: Vasculitis:
list.snippet: The inflammation of blood vessels is a hallmark of GPA. This can lead to a range of symptoms depending on which vessels are affected.

list.title: Symptoms:
list.snippet: Early symptoms can be vague and mimic a cold or flu, including a runny nose, fever, fatigue, and joint pain. Other potential symptoms include sinus pain, cough, ear pain, hearing loss, skin rashes, and kidney problems.

list.title: Organ Involvement:
list.snippet: GPA can affect many organs, including the lungs, kidneys, sinuses, ears, and eyes.

list.title: Diagnosis:
list.snippet: GPA is diagnosed through a combination of clinical evaluation, blood tests (including ANCA testing), and imaging studies.

list.title: Treatment:
list.snippet: Treatment typically involves immunosuppressant drugs, such as corticosteroids, to control inflammation and prevent organ damage.

list.title: Prognosis:
list.snippet: With early diagnosis and treatment, many people with GPA can achieve remission and lead relatively normal lives. However, relapses can occur, and ongoing monitoring is necessary.

list.title: Prevalence:
list.snippet: GPA is a rare disease, and while it can affect people of all ages, it is most commonly diagnosed in individuals between 40 and 65 years old.
